content: 1. Streptomycin administration can lead to both vestibular and auditory dysfunction. The severity of these impairments is directly related to the dose and duration of streptomycin use, the patient’s age, renal function, and any pre-existing auditory dysfunction. 2. The ototoxic effects of aminoglycosides, including streptomycin, are exacerbated when co-administered with ethacrynic acid, mannitol, furosemide, and possibly other diuretics. 3. Streptomycin has a greater potential for vestibulotoxicity compared to cochlear toxicity. Vestibular damage is often preceded by symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, and disequilibrium. 4. Early cochlear injury is typically indicated by the loss of high-frequency hearing. Proper monitoring and early discontinuation of the drug may allow recovery before irreversible damage to the sensorineural cells occurs. 5. Streptomycin can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Since it readily crosses the placental barrier, its use during pregnancy requires caution to prevent ototoxicity in the fetus. 6. If streptomycin is used during pregnancy or if a patient becomes pregnant while taking the drug, the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. 7. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including streptomycin. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. 8. Antibacterial treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. 9. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A thorough medical history is essential, as CDAD can occur up to two months after antibiotic administration. 10. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be initiated as clinically indicated. 11. Streptomycin should not be prescribed in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria without providing benefit to the patient. 12. Baseline and periodic caloric stimulation tests and audiometric tests are recommended during extended streptomycin therapy. Symptoms such as tinnitus, roaring noises, or a sense of fullness in the ears necessitate audiometric examination or discontinuation of therapy, or both. 13. Individuals handling streptomycin for injection should take precautions to avoid skin sensitivity reactions. 14. Streptomycin sulfate injection should be administered deep into a large muscle to minimize the risk of peripheral nerve damage. Extreme caution is required when selecting a dosage regimen in patients with pre-existing renal insufficiency. 15. In severely uremic patients, a single dose of streptomycin may result in high blood levels for several days, and cumulative effects may lead to ototoxic sequelae. 16. Prolonged streptomycin use may require alkalinization of the urine to minimize or prevent renal irritation. 17. In very young infants, excessive streptomycin dosage has been associated with central nervous system depression, characterized by stupor, flaccidity, occasional coma, and deep respiratory depression. Infants should not receive streptomycin in excess of the recommended dosage. 18. In the treatment of venereal infections such as granuloma inguinale and chancroid, if concomitant syphilis is suspected, appropriate laboratory procedures (e.g., dark field examination) should be performed before starting treatment, and monthly serologic tests should be conducted for at least four months. 19. As with other antibiotics, streptomycin use may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, appropriate therapy should be instituted. 20. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including streptomycin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). 21. When prescribed for a bacterial infection, patients should be informed that although they may feel better early in the course of therapy, the medication should be taken exactly as directed. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may decrease the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance. 22. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even two or more months after completing the antibiotic course. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician promptly. 23. Streptomycin is classified as Pregnancy Category D. Refer to the Warnings section for further details. 24. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 25. For pediatric use, refer to the Dosage and Administration section.
